title: Pauri 25, sound: bahutaa karam
tomorrow: Pauri 25, meaning: even hunger is a gift

segments.voice: Yesterday, no end to praise. Your line was the more remains. Did you thank someone, and find there was more to thank them for? Today, the end of a week, and a stanza about giving. Day two hundred three.

Look back at this week. Paataalaa paataal, the endless elevator. The writing runs out. Saalaahee, the praisers who never grasp it all. Be the ant. Ant na siftee, and the more remains. Every day, a way of saying: too big for us. Now picture a grandmother who cooks for everyone who walks through the door. You ask her how much she's made. She laughs. She's never counted. Keeping score isn't how she thinks. Pauri 25 starts with a giver like that.
screen: `THE WEEK: ENDLESS, UNWRITTEN, THE ANT.` → `A GRANDMOTHER WHO COOKS FOR ALL.` → `SHE'S NEVER COUNTED.`

segments.voice: Here's the first line of Pauri 25 in the original: bahutaa karam likhiaa naa jaae. Bahutaa: so much, so great. You heard it yesterday: bahutaa aakheeai bahutaa hoe. Karam: and here's a word to be careful with. It looks like karma, but Sikh commentators read karam here as a different word, from Persian and Arabic, meaning generosity, kindness, grace. Not what you've done, but what's given to you. Likhiaa: written. Naa jaae: cannot be. So: His generosity is so great it cannot be written down. That's the same honesty as the last few stanzas, the writing runs out, but now about giving. The next line, in paraphrase: the great Giver doesn't have even a sesame seed of greed. There's til again, the sesame seed from Pauri 21. The Giver wants nothing back, not even that much. Listen to the rhythm. Bahutaa karam, two strong beats, a lift. Likhiaa naa jaae, falling softly, like setting something down. It's an easy line to carry. Sikh practice has its own picture of a giver who doesn't count. The langar, the gurdwara's free kitchen, feeds anyone who comes, of any faith or none, sitting together on the floor, and nobody tallies who ate. Tomorrow we'll hear where the stanza goes, and it goes somewhere surprising, to hunger and pain. Today, just the sound. Bahutaa karam: so much giving it can't be written.
screen: `BAHUTAA — SO MUCH.` · `KARAM — GENEROSITY, GRACE.` · `NOT A SESAME SEED OF GREED.` · `THE LANGAR DOESN'T COUNT.` · then, large: `BAHUTAA KARAM.`

segments.voice: Say the first line aloud: bahutaa karam, likhiaa naa jaae. Once slowly, feeling the lift and the fall. Twice more, softer. Then sit and bring to mind three things you were given this week that you didn't earn: a smile, a meal, a kind word, a sunrise. Don't count them up. Just let them arrive. The bell holds the time.
Karam, generosity, grace. It opens bahutaa karam, likhiaa naa jaae: His generosity is so great it cannot be written.
Your line: bahutaa karam. Today, give one thing without keeping score: a coffee, a favor, your time, and don't mention it. Day two hundred three.

fork.reveal: vaddaa daataa til na tamaae: the great Giver hasn't a sesame seed of greed. the giving can't even be written down.

original.note: Gurmukhi, Japji Pauri 25, line 1: His generosity is so great it cannot be written.

trapdoor: what you thought: karam means karma, what you've done.
what it means: karam here is generosity, grace: what's given, so much it can't be written.
what a scholar hears: commentators take karam in this line from Persian/Arabic karam, generosity, rather than Sanskrit karma; til, the sesame seed, returns from Pauri 21.
